definition: Triplet loss is a machine learning loss function widely used in one-shot learning, a setting where models are trained to generalize effectively from limited examples.
details: It was conceived by Google researchers for their prominent FaceNet algorithm for face detection. Triplet loss is designed to support metric learning. Namely, to assist training models to learn an embedding (mapping to a feature space) where similar data points are closer together and dissimilar ones are farther apart, enabling robust discrimination across varied conditions. In the context of face detection, data points correspond to images.

explainer.lead: Triplet loss is a loss function widely used in one-shot learning, where models must generalise from few examples. It matters because it trains embeddings in which similar points sit close and dissimilar points sit far apart.

tiers.eli5: You show the model three things at once: an anchor, something like it, and something different; the model learns to keep the look-alikes together and push the odd one away.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers train with anchor, positive and negative samples to learn a metric space for verification and retrieval; a common pitfall is hard or careless triplet selection, since uninformative negatives stall learning.
tiers.paperLevel: Triplet loss supports metric learning by learning an embedding where similar data points are closer and dissimilar ones farther apart; it was conceived by Google researchers for FaceNet.

explainer.example: For face detection, an anchor image of a person is paired with another photo of the same person (positive) and a photo of someone else (negative), and the embedding is pushed so the positive is closer than the negative.
